title: HPV vaccine-related articles shared on Facebook from 2019 to 2021: Did COVID make a difference?
screen_reason: Content analysis of 138 HPV vaccine-related articles shared on Facebook in 2019–2021, with an explicit false-statement codebook: 41% (n = 56) contained some type of misinformation, with per-year values of 50%, 44% and 24%. A quantitative share of items with a stated denominator and an external falsity criterion, so eligible.

estimates.country: Not restricted; English-language articles from U.S. and international news outlets, national and local
estimates.platform: Facebook (articles shared on Facebook, indexed by Buzzsumo)
estimates.date: articles shared on Facebook 2019–2021 (50 highest-engagement English-language articles per year)
estimates.measure_type: % of the highest-engagement HPV vaccine-related articles shared on Facebook that contained any misinformation
estimates.value_raw: In total, 41% of the articles (n = 56) contained some type of misinformation [per year: 2019 25/50 = 50%, 2020 22/50 = 44%, 2021 9/38 = 24%]
estimates.denominator: 138 English-language HPV-related articles shared on Facebook (the 50 highest-engagement articles for 2019 and 2020 and the 38 articles from 2021 with engagement scores above 1000), collected with Buzzsumo; engagement = total reactions, comments and shares, ranging from 1,095 to 236,841
estimates.definition: Article coded at the sentence level as containing at least one false statement about the HPV vaccine, in any of five codes: death, neurological effects, harmful chemicals, fertility effects, or other misinformation (“False statement about harmful side effects of the vaccine not in other categories or other obviously false statement about the HPV vaccine or HPV in general”)
estimates.misinfo_def: “False statement about the HPV vaccine causing death or carrying a risk of death”; “False statement about the HPV vaccine causing severe or life-altering neurological issues”; “False statement about harmful chemicals being in the HPV vaccine”; “False statement about the HPV vaccine causing infertility or negatively affecting fertility”; “False statement about harmful side effects of the vaccine not in other categories or other obviously false statement about the HPV vaccine or HPV in general”

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three authors (LAS, AM, EA) group-coded five articles to build the codebook, then coded 20 articles for interrater reliability (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.811), resolved differences by consensus, and each remaining article was coded independently by one of the three; coding done in Atlas.ti Web, analysis in SPSS 29
estimates.moderator_quote: Articles were prioritized by engagement scores provided by Buzzsumo, defined as the total number of reactions, comments, and shares. For each of the three years, we collected 50 English-language articles with the highest engagement scores. To focus on articles with high engagement, we excluded articles with engagement scores of <1000.
estimates.notes: CONSTRUCT JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator. Coded SHARING / content_share because the denominator is items selected for having been shared and engaged with on Facebook (the protocol's “% of shared links unreliable is SHARING, not CONTENT” rule), not all HPV articles that exist. The competing reading is CONTENT: each article is a unique document coded once, engagement is only the selection rule, and the paper presents itself as a content analysis. The choice matters because the sample is the extreme top of the engagement distribution (minimum 1,095 engagements), so this is the misinformation rate among the most-shared HPV articles, which is not the rate in an average Facebook feed. TIME SERIES: collapsed to the pooled 2019–2021 total (41%) as the representative point; per-year values are in value_raw. year coded 2020 as the midpoint of the 2019–2021 window. NUMBER PROBLEM: the text and abstract report the year trend as p = 0.04, but the Table 2 chi-square for “Misinformation (any)” reads 0.37; the paper also gives positive valence as n = 72; 52% in the text and 71 (51%) in Table 2 and the abstract. Neither affects the 41% value but both bear on RoB.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) Per-year misinformation shares (2019 50%, 2020 44%, 2021 24%): a time series, collapsed to the pooled total per protocol; all three are recorded in value_raw. (2) Misinformation subtype shares (death 22% n=30, neurological effects 19% n=26, harmful chemicals 10% n=14, fertility effects 7% n=10, other misinformation 36% n=50): non-mutually-exclusive sub-codes of the same measure; extracting them would breach R4 and they cannot be summed. An adjudicator wanting a stricter definitional variant should take “death” (22%) as the narrowest. (3) Valence shares (positive 51%, negative 36%, mixed 13%): a stance measure, not a veracity measure; an anti-vaccine article is not thereby false. (4) “6% of positive valence articles, compared to 90% of negative valence articles containing misinformation (p < 0.001)”: a subgroup breakdown by an internal coding variable, not the paper's headline and not a demographic/party split. (5) Persuasive tactic, evidence type, framing and topic shares (mistrust of institutions 30%, fear appeal 30%, ideological assertion 26%, personal narrative 29%, statistics 74%, cancer-prevention framing 70%, etc.): rhetorical features, not falsity. (6) Article source shares (news 46%, advocacy 13%, government/medical 7%, other 33%; 14 of 19 advocacy articles from Children's Health Defense): corpus composition. (7) The Discussion cites an external report that the “Disinformation Dozen” produced over 65% of anti-vaccine content online and over 73% on Facebook: a figure from another publication, barred by R8, and a concentration claim that is NOT this paper's own data. (8) Engagement scores 1,095–236,841: a range of engagement, not a misinformation share.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of web articles selected by Facebook engagement. Buzzsumo, a web-crawling social analytics platform, was used to retrieve HPV-related articles shared on Facebook in 2019, 2020 and 2021; for each year the 50 English-language articles with the highest engagement scores (reactions + comments + shares) were taken, with articles under 1,000 engagements excluded, which left only 38 articles for 2021 and a total sample of 138. Codebook built by three authors group-coding five articles; interrater reliability computed on 20 articles (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.811) with disagreements resolved by consensus; the remaining articles were each coded by a single author, so most of the corpus was single-coded. Misinformation was coded at sentence level in five non-mutually-exclusive categories and aggregated to the document level. Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests, SPSS 29, alpha = 0.05. Stated limitations: Facebook privacy changes meant the authors could not see the text of the sharing posts, the comments, or any demographics of the people who engaged. Two internal inconsistencies: the misinformation-by-year p-value is 0.04 in the text and abstract but 0.37 in Table 2, and positive valence is 72 (52%) in the text but 71 (51%) in Table 2 and the abstract.
rob.item6_quote: We coded for any misinformation about the HPV vaccine. We specifically coded for each instance of misinformation related to death, neurological effects, harmful chemicals, fertility effects, and other types of misinformation.
